item.title: Criteria of Value: Auteurism as Late Classical Film Theory
item.description:
Authors: Mynt Marsellus

Source: Stanford Humanities Center

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Andrew Sarris and Pauline Kael’s debate over the value of the auteur theory is frequently historicized as a debate over the value of authorship study as such. This essay, through a close reading of “Notes on the Auteur Theory in 1962” and “Circles and Squares,” argues instead that their disagreement is better understood as concerning the value of cinema and cinema culture more broadly. Sarris argues for auteurism as a method of expanding the recognition of cinema’s value as a major art, while Kael argues that theoretical models always simplify the lively humanistic work of aesthetic culture.

item.title: Analysis of sustainable development: an overlapping generations model of agricultural households in developing countries
item.description:
Authors: Abel Kutangila

Source: Environment and Development Economics

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Abstract This article examines the effectiveness of individual transferable quotas (ITQs) in promoting sustainable resource management within an overlapping generations economy where agricultural producers face credit constraints. The analysis shows that, although ITQs restore the social optimum when markets are complete, their effectiveness breaks down when credit constraints bind. Credit frictions create a wedge between the marginal product of the resource and its effective price, leading constrained agents to underinvest in quotas and generating resource misallocation. As a result, ITQs alone are insufficient to ensure environmental preservation without compromising welfare. The study therefore shows that policies improving credit access, such as loan guarantees, are necessary complements to ITQ systems if sustainable resource management is to be achieved.

item.title: Neurodegenerative disease risk associated with gene expression in peripheral monocytes across ancestries
item.description:

Source: Communications Biology

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Abstract It is hypothesised that peripheral immune states responding to regional environmental triggers contribute to central neurodegeneration. Region-specific genetic selection pressures require this hypothesis to be assessed in an ancestry-specific manner. Here, we utilise genome-wide association studies and expression quantitative trait loci from African, East Asian and European ancestries to show that genes causally-implicated in neurodegeneration are preferentially expressed in innate rather than adaptive immune cells. Using colocalisation and Mendelian randomisation analyses, we show that in addition to known colocalising signals in microglia, genetic variants associated with neurodegenerative disease risk also regulate the expression of these genes in peripheral monocytes across ancestries.
